Prepare Your Hearts! Miguel Lallo and Diego Lira Meet With the Cast of 'Heartstopper' in London to Announce the Premiere of 'Here the Whole Time' on Netflix
summary: Netflix heard the fans loud and clear! Here the Whole Time, an adaptation of Vitor Martins's bestseller starring Miguel Lallo and Diego Lira, will be available for streaming worldwide on August 19.
body_text: São Paulo, July 14, 2026 — Netflix heard the fans loud and clear! Here the Whole Time , an adaptation of Vitor Martins's bestseller starring Miguel Lallo and Diego Lira, will be available for streaming worldwide on August 19 . To celebrate the news, Netflix brought the stars of the movie to London for a get-together with Kit Connor and Joe Locke, stars of the feature Heartstopper Forever , which premieres on July 17 and marks the end of the hit franchise inspired by Alice Oseman's graphic novel. (Photo Credit: Netflix) Based on books that have captivated readers around the world, Here the Whole Time – which fans lovingly call the “ Brazilian Heartstopper” — and the UK show share themes such as youth, LGBTQIA+ identity, belonging and the discoveries of first love. The actors' meeting highlighted the connection between the stories and celebrated the new Netflix releases. After moving audiences in theaters, Here the Whole Time will be available to watch, rewatch and binge on Netflix whenever you want, as many times as you like, starting August 19. About Here the Whole Time Synopsis: Felipe (Miguel Lallo), a sensitive teenager with a passion for pop culture, just wants to survive the summer break — staying away from the school bullies, binge-watching his favorite shows and forgetting about the outside world. But his plans go awry when his self-assured neighbor Caio (Diego Lira), the popular guy at school and his old crush, moves in under the same roof for two weeks. About Heartstopper Forever Synopsis: Nick (Kit Connor) and Charlie (Joe Locke) are inseparable, but with Nick about to leave for university and Charlie discovering a new independence at school, the reality of a long-distance relationship starts to weigh on them. Doubts begin to set in, and their relationship faces its biggest challenge yet. Meanwhile, the couple's friends are also navigating the ups and downs of love and friendship, facing the pains and joys of growing up and forging their own paths. Can first love really last forever? About Conspiração Conspiração is one of Brazil’s leading independent production companies, founded by filmmakers and built around Brazilian artistic creation. With 10 International Emmy nominations – the most for any independent production company in Latin America – Conspiração co-produced I'm Still Here , winner of the Academy Award® for Best International Feature Film and the Golden Globe® for Best Actress – Drama. The production company is also behind five of the biggest box office hits in Brazilian cinema. Conspiração's projects have premiered at major international festivals, including Cannes, Berlin, Sundance, Venice, and Toronto. With more than 50 feature films, 30 series, and 45 documentaries produced, totaling more than 30 million tickets sold at the box office and over 300 awards, the company combines a strong artistic vision with projects that reach both Brazilian audiences and the international market, rooted in the strength of Brazilian storytelling. About Manequim Filmes Manequim Filmes, Vitrine group's commercial distribution label, was created to bring the best of Brazilian cinema to wider audiences. In just three years, Manequim has already established itself in the audiovisual market with Brazil’s highest-grossing national release of 2023: Our Dream – The Story of Claudinho and Buchecha . In 2026, it released The King of the Internet , the story of Brazilian hacker Daniel Nascimento and Here the Whole Time , based on the bestseller by Vítor Martins. The Vitrine Filmes Group has distributed more than 300 films over the course of more than 15 years. Its biggest successes include The Secret Agent, Bacurau , Invisible Life and The Way He Looks . Its documentary releases include Pictures of Ghosts , Divine Divas , The Trial and Secret Friend . About Netflix Netflix is one of the world’s leading entertainment services offering TV series, films, games and live programming across a wide variety of genres and languages. Members can play, pause and resume watching as much as they want, anytime, anywhere, and can change their plans at any time. Press Kit Agência Ágora | netflix@agora.site

title: Startup PR vs LinkedIn for Founders: Where Credibility Actually Compounds
summary: Startup PR can create useful credibility spikes, but LinkedIn gives founders the repeatable surface where trust compounds before buyers, investors, and candidates are ready to act.
body_text: Startup PR vs LinkedIn for Founders: Where Credibility Actually Compounds Startup PR has a clean story. A founder gets quoted in a respected publication. The company announces a raise. A product launch gets covered. The logo goes on the website. Investors notice. Candidates see momentum. Buyers get a third-party signal that the company is real. That signal matters. But most founders overestimate what PR can do by itself. Press can create a spike of attention. It can validate a moment. It can make a company easier to trust when someone is already looking. What it usually cannot do is build a repeated relationship with the market every week. That is where LinkedIn is different. LinkedIn is not a replacement for startup PR. It is the place where the founder turns market judgment into repeated visibility. PR says someone noticed you. LinkedIn shows why the market should keep paying attention. This guide breaks down startup PR vs LinkedIn for founders: what each channel is good at, where each one fails, when to invest in PR, when to prioritize founder-led LinkedIn, and how to make the two work together without turning the founder into a full-time content operator. ‍ What Startup PR Actually Does Startup PR is public relations for startups: media relationships, announcements, founder commentary, thought leadership placements, podcast appearances, analyst mentions, awards, and other third-party visibility. The strongest PR creates borrowed credibility. A buyer may not know the company, but they know the publication. An investor may not have met the founder, but they see market validation. A candidate may not understand the category, but they see momentum from outside the company's own website. That is useful because early and growth-stage companies have a trust deficit. The product may be strong, but the market has not had enough time to decide whether the company matters. PR can shorten that distance. For founders, PR is especially useful around moments: funding announcements, major customer wins, category shifts, original data, executive hires, product launches, partnerships, and strong points of view on a timely market story. The mistake is treating PR like a permanent demand engine. A press hit can create attention. It does not automatically create a content system, a sales narrative, or a founder voice the market learns to recognize. ‍ Why Founders Overestimate PR Founders overestimate PR because press feels concrete. There is a headline. There is a link. There is a logo. There may be a traffic spike, a few investor texts, and a burst of employee excitement. Compared with the slow compounding of founder-led content, PR feels like a win you can point to. But the shelf life is short. Most articles get one wave of distribution. The audience sees the story, reacts if it matters, and moves on. Unless the company has a way to keep the conversation alive, the press hit becomes a credibility artifact instead of a growth channel. PR also depends on external timing. A founder can have a strong story and still lose the cycle to bigger news. A reporter can be interested and still never publish. A launch can be meaningful to the company but not newsworthy to the market. That does not make PR bad. It makes PR episodic. Founders get into trouble when they expect an episodic channel to do a compounding channel's job. PR can validate a moment. LinkedIn can turn that moment into repeated market education. ‍ What LinkedIn Does That PR Cannot LinkedIn gives founders control over the cadence. A founder does not need a reporter to approve a post about a customer pattern, a category belief, a hiring lesson, a sales objection, or a product decision. They can publish directly to the market and see what happens. That speed matters because B2B trust is built through repetition. Buyers rarely change their mind because of one article. Investors rarely build conviction from one quote. Candidates rarely decide a founder is worth following from one announcement. They need repeated exposure to how the founder thinks. LinkedIn makes that possible. A founder can explain the problem before the buyer is ready to buy. They can make the category feel urgent before the sales team reaches out. They can show judgment before a fundraising process starts. They can answer objections in public before those objections show up on calls. This is the same reason founder-led marketing works. The founder becomes the clearest carrier of the company's market belief, because the founder is closest to the customer, product, category, and risk. PR can amplify credibility. LinkedIn can manufacture familiarity. ‍ Startup PR vs LinkedIn: The Real Difference The real difference is not earned media versus social media. The real difference is borrowed trust versus repeated trust. Startup PR borrows trust from a publication, podcast, analyst, community, or third-party voice. That borrowed trust is valuable when the audience respects the source. It can help a young company look more legitimate faster. LinkedIn builds repeated trust through the founder's own voice. The market sees the founder make claims, explain tradeoffs, respond to comments, share customer patterns, and take a position over time. The trust is not borrowed. It is earned in public. Both matter, but they solve different problems. Use PR when the company has a moment the market should notice. Use LinkedIn when the founder has a point of view the market should remember. Use PR to make a milestone more credible. Use LinkedIn to explain why the milestone matters. Use PR when a third-party source can validate the company. Use LinkedIn when the founder needs to teach the market how to think about the problem. The best B2B founders do not choose one forever. They know which job they are hiring each channel to do. ‍ When Startup PR Wins Startup PR wins when third-party validation matters more than direct explanation. Funding is the obvious example. A raise is not just capital. It is a market signal. A good funding announcement can support investor relations, recruiting, customer confidence, and partner interest. LinkedIn can distribute the story, but the outside coverage gives it weight. PR also wins when the company has original data. If a startup can show a market shift with credible numbers, a reporter or industry publication can help the insight travel beyond the founder's immediate network. PR is useful for category moments. When regulation changes, a new platform launches, a market breaks, or a well-known company creates a debate, a founder with a sharp take can become part of the public conversation. PR helps with legitimacy in conservative markets. Enterprise buyers, public-sector buyers, financial services buyers, and risk-sensitive categories often care about external proof. A strong press footprint can reduce the feeling that the company is too unknown. PR can also help with executive recruiting. Senior candidates want to know whether the company has momentum. Coverage gives them something to inspect beyond the careers page. In all of those cases, PR is doing the job it should do: creating external validation around a real moment. ‍ When LinkedIn Wins LinkedIn wins when the market needs repetition, education, and founder trust. If buyers do not fully understand the problem yet, LinkedIn is stronger than PR. The founder can explain the pain from different angles every week. They can name the pattern buyers feel but have not articulated. They can make the category more urgent through repeated examples. If the company sells into a long B2B sales cycle, LinkedIn is stronger. Buyers may not be ready today, but they can still become familiar with the founder's thinking long before procurement starts. If the founder's judgment is part of the sale, LinkedIn is stronger. This is common in founder-led companies, technical products, new categories, and high-trust services. Buyers want to know whether the founder actually understands the market. If fundraising visibility matters, LinkedIn is stronger between announcements. PR can support the raise when the moment arrives. LinkedIn builds the track record investors quietly watch before the meeting. That connects directly to what investors look for in a founder's LinkedIn . If sales needs warmer context, LinkedIn is stronger. A founder post can become an outbound opener, a follow-up asset, an objection handler, or a reason for a buyer to accept a connection. That is why founder-led sales on LinkedIn is not just posting. It is sales context created before the pitch. LinkedIn wins when the work is not one big announcement. It wins when the market needs to hear the same founder make the same sharp point in enough ways that it finally sticks. ‍ The Best Workflow Uses Both The strongest workflow is not PR or LinkedIn. It is PR plus founder-led distribution. Before a PR moment, the founder should use LinkedIn to prepare the market. If a funding announcement is coming, publish the category thesis before the round is public. If a product launch is coming, explain the customer problem and the old way that is breaking. If original data is coming, test the underlying narrative in posts first. During the PR moment, LinkedIn should translate the headline into founder thinking. Do not just repost the article with a generic caption. Explain what the milestone reveals, why the company made the bet, what customer pattern led to it, and what the market should understand next. After the PR moment, LinkedIn should keep the story alive. Break the coverage into smaller ideas. Turn the founder quote into a post. Turn the customer problem into a series. Turn the data into sales enablement. Turn the announcement into recruiting context. This is how PR stops being a one-day spike and becomes part of a larger content system. A single press hit can support weeks of founder-led content if the team knows how to extract the underlying point of view. ‍ How to Decide Where to Invest First Founders should invest first in the channel that matches the current constraint. If the company lacks credibility around a major milestone, PR may be the right move. A strong announcement can make the market take the company more seriously. If the company lacks a clear narrative, LinkedIn should come first. PR cannot fix a weak point of view. If the founder cannot explain what the market gets wrong, why the problem matters, and why the company is credible, press will only expose the lack of clarity. If the company needs pipeline, LinkedIn usually comes first. PR can create awareness, but founder-led LinkedIn is better at building repeated familiarity with buyers and giving sales usable context. If the company needs investor awareness months before a raise, LinkedIn comes first. PR is useful when there is news. LinkedIn is useful before there is news. If the company has original data or a genuinely timely market angle, PR may come first. But the LinkedIn plan should be ready before the story goes live. The practical rule is simple: PR works better when the founder already has a point of view. LinkedIn is how that point of view gets built, tested, and sharpened. ‍ What to Measure Do not measure PR and LinkedIn with the same scoreboard. For PR, track the quality of the placement, relevance of the audience, referral traffic, branded search lift, investor or customer replies, candidate mentions, sales usage, and whether the story created a credibility asset the team can reuse. For LinkedIn, track profile views, follower quality, comments from the right people, DMs, connection requests, sales-call mentions, target-account engagement, investor familiarity, and topic patterns that create pipeline signal. The shared question is whether the channel moved the right people closer. That is the same lens behind LinkedIn ROI for founders . The value is not always visible in a clean attribution report. Sometimes it shows up as a warmer reply, a faster investor meeting, a candidate who already understands the mission, or a buyer who says they have been following the founder for months. PR and LinkedIn both create trust. The mistake is pretending trust always converts on the same day it is created. ‍ Common Mistakes Founders Make The first mistake is using PR before the narrative is ready. If the story is vague, press will not make it sharper. The second mistake is treating a press hit as the finish line. The coverage is the start of distribution, not the end. The third mistake is reposting articles without founder commentary. A link alone does not teach the market anything. The founder has to explain why the story matters. The fourth mistake is chasing publications the buyer does not read. A smaller industry placement can be more useful than a broad startup mention if the right operators see it. The fifth mistake is outsourcing the founder's point of view. A PR team can pitch. A content team can edit. But the market needs the founder's real judgment, not a sanitized quote that sounds like every other startup announcement. The sixth mistake is separating PR, sales, and LinkedIn. If sales does not know which story is live, they cannot use it. If LinkedIn does not extend the story, it fades. If PR does not understand the founder's public narrative, it pitches disconnected moments. The channels should reinforce one another. ‍ How Rethoric Thinks About PR and LinkedIn Rethoric's view is that PR is strongest when it has founder-led content around it. The founder should not show up only when there is an announcement. By then, the market has no context. The best founders build the context first. They publish the category thesis, customer patterns, hard lessons, product beliefs, and market frustrations before the press cycle needs them. Then, when PR lands, the audience already has a reason to care. That requires a system. Founders need a way to capture raw thinking, turn it into sharp posts, approve without slowing down, schedule consistently, engage with the right people, tag content by theme, and measure which ideas create business signal. That is what keeps founder-led LinkedIn from becoming random posting. It also makes PR more useful, because every external mention has a stronger narrative to plug into. PR gives the market proof that something happened. LinkedIn helps the founder explain what it means. ‍ The Bottom Line on Startup PR vs LinkedIn Startup PR and LinkedIn are not enemies. They are different trust tools. PR creates credibility spikes around moments that deserve outside validation. LinkedIn creates repeated familiarity with the founder's judgment before buyers, investors, candidates, and partners are ready to act. If you only do PR, the market may notice you and forget why it should care. If you only do LinkedIn, you may build familiarity but miss moments where third-party validation would strengthen the story. The strongest founders use LinkedIn to build the point of view, PR to validate important moments, and founder-led content to keep the story alive after the headline fades. title: Virtual Event Production: 7-Step Guide, Tools & Strategies
summary: Avoid low participation and disengaged audiences. This guide covers key steps, tools & common pitfalls for high-quality virtual event production.
body_text: Without the right tools and strategy, your virtual event could yield high registration numbers but low participation, flat presentations that don’t hold attention, and missed follow-up opportunities. To avoid wasted investment and results that reflect poorly on your decision-making, your approach needs to address not only professional production quality but also a streamlined end-to-end workflow that considers everything from setup to post-event follow-up. This guide walks you through the key steps of virtual event production, from defining goals and choosing the right platform to audience engagement and post-event follow-up. You’ll also learn common mistakes to avoid and how to optimize your event for maximum ROI. Whether you’re focused on lead generation, customer education, or brand positioning, this guide will help you plan, execute, and refine a high-performing virtual event. What is virtual event production? Components, benefits & objectives Virtual event production is the process of planning, executing, and managing an event hosted online using digital tools and technology. It requires a combination of: Broadcast-quality content Audience engagement strategies Engagement and performance analytics When these core elements work together effectively, you create a professional, interactive experience that keeps attendees engaged, whether your event is live or on-demand. Key benefits of virtual event production Virtual events enable you to create engaging, data-driven webinars and digital experiences that support pipeline growth, customer education, and brand positioning. Here’s how they can help you achieve these goals: Scalable processes: Automation and interactive tools streamline event management, allowing you to engage more attendees without added workload. Continued value: Recorded sessions, interactive discussions, and on-demand access ensure your key messaging resonates long after the event ends. Built-in data and analytics: Real-time insights into audience behavior, session performance, and engagement trends allow for continual optimization. Audience targeting: With flexible formatting and integrated marketing tools, you can tailor content for specific industries, job roles, or stages in the buyer journey. Primary goals and objectives A strong virtual event strategy is outcome-driven, with clear objectives that align with business and marketing priorities. Audience engagement: Keeping attendees involved through interactive features like Q&As, polls, and networking sessions creates a more memorable, positive experience. Lead generation: Virtual events provide multiple touchpoints for capturing qualified leads and guiding them through the sales funnel with targeted content. Brand positioning: By delivering valuable insights and high-quality content, you can establish your brand as an authority on relevant topics and solutions. Post-event nurturing: Recorded sessions, personalized follow-ups, and attendee insights help sustain relationships and move attendees further along the customer journey. 💡 Pro tip: Use Demio AI to automate Q&As and chat moderation so you can make personalized follow-ups based on what your audience really care about. This will give on-demand attendees a fully engaging experience and help you continually capture leads from your events. 7-Step guide to virtual event production This guide breaks down the key stages of virtual event production, from setting goals and choosing a platform to audience engagement and post-event follow-up. 1. Define your event goals and ICP Your event’s goals and audience determine key success metrics like registrant-to-attendee conversion, engagement rate, and post-event actions. These decisions shape content structure, speaker selection, and audience interaction, directly impacting ROI. Set a clear objective: Define whether your event is for lead generation, customer education, brand awareness, or networking to shape your content and structure. Narrow down your ideal audience: Identify job roles, industries, experience levels, and pain points to define your ideal audience. Use Reach for audience acquisition: Reach by Banzai helps you attract high-quality attendees that fit your ICP, so the right people show up and participate. Align content with ICP priorities: For executives, focus on high-level insights; for practitioners, include tactical and hands-on content. Use Reach to identify leads, manage your pipeline, and deploy multi-channel outbound campaigns. 2. Choose the right virtual event platform Your virtual event platform determines how easily attendees can register, join, and engage, impacting metrics like attendance rate, session duration, and post-event interactions. Choosing a unified virtual event platform that integrates audience acquisition, hosting, and post-event analytics simplifies execution and maximizes your ROI. Here’s what to prioritize: Ease of use: A seamless registration process and intuitive interface reduce drop-off rates and create a smooth hosting experience. Engagement features: Choose a platform with Q&A, polls, chat, audience reactions, and slide sharing for both live and on-demand webinars. Built-in analytics: Track attendance, session duration, and engagement metrics to measure success and refine future events. Banzai’s full-stack solution: Demio powers virtual event production with automated registration, engagement tools, and post-event analytics, Reach drives audience acquisition, and Boost amplifies event promotion—all within the Banzai ecosystem. Banzai’s family of webinar tools also includes Openreel for branded video creation and management and Vidello’s video marketing suite—so you can seamlessly create, promote, host, and analyze events with a fully integrated, end-to-end event production solution. Demio’s engagement features, automated processes, and AI solutions make virtual event production simple to execute and highly effective. 3. Plan and structure your event content A well-structured event keeps attendees engaged and ensures your key messages are delivered effectively. Thoughtful planning helps maintain momentum, balance speaker contributions, and encourage audience interaction. Here’s how to develop and structure your content: Outline the attendee journey : Define the flow from registration to post-event follow-up, ensuring each segment reinforces your core message and encourages participation. Break sessions into digestible segments: Use a mix of keynotes, panels, breakout sessions, and interactive discussions to maintain engagement while keeping messaging clear and consistent. Incorporate engagement touchpoints: Plan how to integrate Q&As, polls, and interactive chat at key moments to keep attendees actively involved. Match the format to the event type: Webinars, panel discussions, workshops, and product demos each require different content structures—use slide sharing, polls, and speaker prompts to reinforce key takeaways and drive your desired actions. 4. Set up technical requirements and production tools A strong virtual event setup goes beyond choosing the right platform—it’s about optimizing and automating every step to ensure a high-quality attendee experience and reduce manual work for your team. Using natively integrated solutions lets you streamline workflows from registration to follow-up, keeping everything connected without switching between systems. Configure integrations for seamless data flow: Connect your CRM, marketing automation, and analytics tools to sync attendee engagement, track conversions, and automate follow-ups. Automate event setup and attendee experience: Use pre-set event templates, branded registration pages, and automated reminders to minimize admin tasks and ensure a consistent experience. Optimize branding and messaging across touchpoints: Customize your registration pages, emails, and in-session branding so every interaction reinforces your brand. Simplify speaker and attendee onboarding: Provide a pre-event checklist, guided platform walkthroughs, and automated setup instructions to make participation easy for everyone. 5. Rehearse and prepare speakers Even experienced speakers need preparation to deliver their message clearly and stay within time limits. A well-run rehearsal helps you avoid awkward pauses and manage unforeseen circumstances. Hold a full tech run-through: Run a full tech check to confirm audio, video, slides, and screen-sharing are set up for a professional, polished experience. Set expectations for pacing and timing: Clarify the ideal speaking time per segment and build in transitions to keep energy high. Coach speakers on engagement strategies: Encourage them to acknowledge chat responses, refer to audience questions, and maintain a conversational tone. Have a backup plan : Have a moderator ready to step in if you have a no-show. 6. Engage your audience with interactive elements Virtual events need active participation to hold attention—otherwise, attendees passively tune out or drop off. Plan interactive moments to keep them engaged. Use polls and Q&A strategically: Schedule these at key points to break up long presentations and involve the audience. Leverage chat and reactions: Encourage real-time discussions and allow attendees to react to key moments. Offer networking opportunities: Chat threads and structured discussions help attendees connect. Incorporate gamification: Leaderboards, giveaways, and interactive challenges add excitement and keep people engaged. 7. Analyze event performance and follow up Review attendee data to identify high-intent leads, refine content for future events, and tailor follow-ups based on engagement levels. Review key event metrics: Look at attendance rates, engagement levels, and Q&A participation to evaluate performance. Gather attendee feedback: Use post-event surveys to identify what worked and what could improve. Repurpose content for continued reach: Turn key insights into blog posts, short video clips, or follow-up emails to extend the event’s impact. Send personalized follow-ups: Nurture attendees with targeted next steps, whether it’s an on-demand replay, exclusive resources, or a demo request. Mistakes to avoid in virtual event production Even experienced event organizers run into avoidable mistakes that hurt engagement and retention. Here are some real-world pitfalls and how to avoid them: Not setting up a backup engagement plan: If audience interaction is low, you need a way to pull them back in. Have pre-planned discussion prompts or a moderator ready to call on attendees directly in chat or Q&A. Underestimating pre-event marketing: Just sending an invite isn’t enough. Use multi-touch promotion—email sequences, LinkedIn posts, and targeted ads—to increase event attendance. Overcomplicating registration: If sign-up requires too many steps, drop-off increases. Simplify registration with auto-fill forms, calendar invites, and a one-click login option for attendees. Ignoring audience fatigue: Long sessions kill engagement. Break content into shorter, high-energy segments and use interactive elements every 10-15 minutes to hold attention. Not repurposing content post-event: A virtual event isn’t just a one-time experience. Clip high-value moments into short video snippets (which is super-easy with OpenReel’s video creation tools ), turn key takeaways into blog posts, and use on-demand access to extend reach. Avoiding these mistakes will increase attendance, keep audiences engaged, and extend the value of your event beyond the live session. Virtual event production: Key strategies to drive ROI A well-executed virtual event goes beyond simply hosting a webinar—it requires strategic planning, audience engagement, and post-event optimization. By setting clear goals, choosing the right platform, and structuring your content for interaction, you can maximize attendance and participation. Avoid common mistakes like focusing too much on registrations over engagement, underestimating pre-event marketing, or ignoring post-event follow-ups. Instead, leverage automation, audience insights, and interactive tools to keep attendees engaged and drive ROI. Whether you’re running a lead generation event, a customer education session, or a thought leadership panel, using a unified platform like Banzai brings together multiple webinar and marketing solutions that simplify execution and reduce your manual workload. With the right approach, your virtual event can be a valuable, high-converting experience for both your attendees and business.

title: XOMA Royalty Announces Closing of Its Acquisition by Ligand
summary: XOMA Royalty has built a significant portfolio of products that are licensed to and being developed by other biotechnology and pharmaceutical companies.  The Company’s portfolio of partner-funded programs spans multiple stages of the…
body_text: Press Releases XOMA Royalty Announces Closing of Its Acquisition by Ligand Download as PDF July 14, 2026 9:00am EDT EMERYVILLE, Calif., July 14, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- XOMA Royalty Corporation today announced that Ligand Pharmaceuticals Incorporated (Nasdaq: LGND) has completed its previously announced acquisition of XOMA Royalty. Pursuant to the terms of the transaction announced on April 27, 2026, Ligand acquired all of the outstanding shares of XOMA Royalty common stock. XOMA Royalty stockholders received $39.00 in cash per share of XOMA Royalty common stock owned. XOMA Royalty stockholders and equity award holders also received one non-transferable Contingent Value Right (“CVR”) per share entitling the holder to receive a portion of 75% of the net proceeds that may result from certain pending litigation at XOMA Royalty. As a result of the transaction completion, XOMA Royalty’s common stock no longer trades on the Nasdaq stock exchange. Leerink Partners served as lead financial advisor, H.C. Wainwright & Co. served as financial advisor, and Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher LLP served as legal advisor to XOMA Royalty. About XOMA Royalty Corporation XOMA Royalty is a biotechnology royalty aggregator playing a distinctive role in helping biotech companies achieve their goal of improving human health. XOMA Royalty acquires the potential future economics associated with pre-commercial and commercial therapeutic candidates that have been licensed to pharmaceutical or biotechnology companies. When XOMA Royalty acquires the future economics, the seller receives non-dilutive, non-recourse funding they can use to advance their internal drug candidate(s) or for general corporate purposes. XOMA Royalty has an extensive and growing portfolio of assets (asset defined as the right to receive potential future economics associated with the advancement of an underlying therapeutic candidate). For more information about XOMA Royalty and its portfolio, please visit www.xoma.com or follow XOMA Royalty Corporation on LinkedIn . Contacts Investors and Media: Maghan Meyers Maghan@argotpartners.com (646) 367-2769 Source: XOMA Royalty Corporation Released July 14, 2026
